Habitat_Description: Clam Bayou (approximately 125 acres) is a shallow, mangrove-lined lagoon located on Sanibel Island between the Pine Island Sound estuary and the Gulf of Mexico, adjacent to the J.N. “Ding” Darling National Wildlife refuge. Water quality, temperature and salinity fluctuate widely due to variations in tidal exchange associated with storm events and pass closings due beach sand transport. . The primary habitats are mangrove wetland and submerged seagrass and mudflat habitats. Primary native vegetation species include red mangroves, white mangroves, black mangroves and shoal grass. The habitats support a wide variety of invertebrates, fish and mammals, including oysters, clams, killifish, mangrove snapper and many crab species. The surrounding land use is in residential and commercial use, with artificial waterways. The connecting pass between Clam Bayou and the Gulf of Mexico frequently opens and closes depending on storm and beach renourishment conditions. When the pass is closed temperature and salinity increase and water quality declines, causing fish kills algae blooms and hypersalinity in the bayou. The city of Sanibel, along with many partners, began a hydrologic restoration project in 2006 to add culverts to assure tidal exchange between the bayou, Pine Island Sound and the Gulf of Mexico. Project_Name: Newman Branch Canal Living Shoreline Tidal Creek Restoration Project
Project_Description: These canals have steep, unstable slopes that could be improved by transforming them into living shorelines.  Ecosphere offered to assist by securing grant funding from the TBEP to design and permit the implementation of a nature-based shoreline stabilization approach.  The resultant design also including creating a tidal creek system behind the former steep shoreline to increase estuarine habitat and provide a nursery ground for juvenile fisheries.  This resultant project not only improves fisheries, it also provides water quality improvements with the addition of the tidal creek system with native estuarine plants that will absorb nutrients. Another successful P3 project!

Project_Description: This project will remove invasive species, primarily Brazilian pepper, and re-create a variety of native estuarine, freshwater, and upland habitats.  The disturbed portion of the site will be re-contoured into productive estuarine habitat by planting roughly 25,000 native plants with volunteers.  At higher elevations, the cleared area will be turned into freshwater ponds. An education signage will be installed when the project is completed to educate the public about the importance of the habitat to fisheries and avifaunal species.  Nearby, and additional component was added which increases mangrove habitat and improves hydrologic connection to saltern areas.
